crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Symptom Triage and Routing
children.blurb: Symptom triage and routing refers to automated systems that collect a patient's reported symptoms, estimate urgency, and direct them to appropriate care settings such as self-care, primary care, urgent care, or emergency services.

children.name: Vital Signs from a Camera
children.blurb: Camera-based vital sign measurement uses ordinary video, typically from a webcam or smartphone, to estimate pulse rate, respiratory rate, and sometimes blood oxygen saturation without contact.

children.name: Wearable Data in Clinical Care
children.blurb: Wearable data in clinical care refers to physiological signals collected outside the clinic by consumer or medical-grade devices, such as heart rate, activity, sleep, blood oxygen, glucose, and single-lead electrocardiograms, and their use in remote monitoring, triage, and chronic disease management.

children.name: Conversational Care and Its Limits
children.blurb: Conversational care in telemedicine and triage covers automated text or voice interfaces that ask patients about symptoms, history, and urgency before a clinician visit.

children.name: Digital Signals of Mental Health
children.blurb: Digital signals of mental health refers to the measurable traces people leave through phones, wearables, telehealth visits, and online activity that may relate to mood, anxiety, sleep, cognition, or risk of self-harm.

sections.body: Telemedicine and triage covers the ways artificial intelligence sorts patients by symptom, measures vital signs without contact, reads data from wearables, conducts text or voice conversations, and flags possible mental health signals. In practice, symptom checkers ask a series of questions and suggest whether a person should seek emergency care, urgent care, or self-care. Camera-based tools analyze subtle color changes in the face to estimate heart rate and breathing rate. Wearable devices send heart rhythm, sleep, and activity data to clinical dashboards for review. Conversational agents collect intake information and follow up after visits. Language models scan typed or spoken responses for words and patterns associated with depression or anxiety.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The field is uneven. Symptom triage tools handle common complaints well but can miss rare or overlapping conditions, and they still require a human to confirm the route. Camera-based vital signs work in good light and still subjects, but accuracy drops with dark skin tones, motion, or poor lighting. Wearable data is noisy, and many clinicians treat it as a screening signal rather than a diagnostic result. Conversational care can manage simple, scripted tasks, but it struggles with vague symptoms, sarcasm, or safety-critical statements. Digital mental health signals from language are early and produce many false positives, and this site tracks 1000 medical AI models and six active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, which shows both the scale of the work and the real consequences when triage or monitoring fails.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: These pages move from the first point of contact to the data that surrounds a patient. Symptom Triage and Routing explains how AI decides where a person should go next, and it is the natural starting point. Vital Signs from a Camera and Wearable Data in Clinical Care then cover two ways of collecting physiological information, one contactless and one continuous. Conversational Care and Its Limits looks at what chatbots and voice agents can and cannot do during an interaction. Digital Signals of Mental Health examines the more speculative use of language and behavior patterns to infer psychological state. A reader would use the first page to understand routing, the next two to compare measurement methods, and the last two to see where interaction and inference still fall short.
